report:
## Honey for Acute Cough in Children: What the Evidence Shows

Yes—current evidence supports honey as a modestly effective, low-risk remedy for acute cough in children **over age 1**, though the certainty of evidence is low to moderate.

**Systematic review evidence:** The most authoritative source is the Cochrane systematic review (Oduwole et al., 2018, updated), which pooled randomized controlled trials comparing honey to placebo, no treatment, or over-the-counter cough medicines in children aged 1–18 with acute upper respiratory infections. It found honey "probably" reduces cough frequency/severity and improves children's (and parents') sleep more than no treatment, with little difference versus dextromethorphan, and moderate-certainty evidence that honey resolved cough sooner than salbutamol (Cochrane, https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD007094_honey-acute-cough-children; Cochrane Library, https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD007094.pub5/full).

A 2023 systematic review in the European Journal of Pediatrics reached a similar conclusion—"low quality evidence" that honey outperforms cough medication or placebo—while noting more rigorous blinded trials are still needed (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10570220/).

**Individual trials**, such as a double-blind, placebo-controlled study in *Pediatrics* (2012) testing three honey types against a placebo syrup, found honey significantly improved nocturnal cough and sleep quality compared to placebo (https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/130/3/465/30142/Effect-of-Honey-on-Nocturnal-Cough-and-Sleep).

**Important caveat—infant botulism:** Honey must never be given to infants under 12 months old, due to risk of Clostridium botulinum spores causing infant botulism (Cleveland Clinic, https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/infant-botulism).

**Bottom line:** For children over 1 year, honey is a reasonable, evidence-supported, low-cost alternative to OTC cough medicines, endorsed by WHO and pediatric guidelines—though evidence quality remains low-to-moderate and better-designed trials are warranted.
